opus-5.5.text:
So I think the right way to understand it is through what people call Moravec's paradox. The things we think of as hard, like playing chess, proving theorems, or doing calculus, have turned out to be relatively easy for computers. But what a one- or two-year-old does without any apparent effort, like picking up a toy, stacking blocks, walking across a cluttered room, or recognizing their mother's face across many lighting conditions, has turned out to be extraordinarily hard to get machines to do.

The reason, I believe, is evolutionary. Perception and motor control have been refined over hundreds of millions of years. Every animal that moves has had to solve these problems to survive. Language and abstract reasoning are, in evolutionary terms, very recent, maybe a few hundred thousand years, maybe less. So the sensorimotor machinery is deeply optimized and mostly unconscious. We don't have introspective access to how we do it, so we underestimate it. Chess feels hard because we're aware of every step of the effort. Grasping a cup feels trivial because the hard work happens below the level of awareness.

And when you look at how children acquire these skills, it's not passive. Babies are little scientists. They're constantly moving, poking, putting things in their mouths, dropping things off high chairs to see what happens. They're running experiments. That sort of embodied, interactive learning, where perception and action are tightly coupled and the child gets feedback from the physical world, is what builds the foundation. Only later, on top of that grounded understanding of objects, space, and physics, do you get language and more abstract cognition.

So the lesson I take for AI is that we shouldn't think of intelligence as starting from language and symbols. The sensorimotor foundation is the hard part, and it comes first, both in evolution and in development. If we want robots that can really operate in the world, we have to take that seriously and figure out how to get machines to learn the way children do, through active exploration, at scale, in the real world.

r002.rationale: It describes babies constantly moving and experimenting, and says this interactive learning builds the sensorimotor foundation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that we systematically underestimate it. There's this old observation, Moravec's paradox, that the things that are hard for humans, like playing chess or doing symbolic integration, turned out to be easy for computers, while the things that every three-year-old does effortlessly, picking up a cup, walking across a cluttered room, recognizing their mother's face from an odd angle, turned out to be extraordinarily hard. And I think the reason is evolutionary. Perception and motor control have been refined over hundreds of millions of years. Abstract reasoning, language, these are maybe a hundred thousand years old. So the brain has had an enormous amount of time to get the sensorimotor stuff right, and that's exactly why it looks easy to us. It's happening below the level of conscious access.

Now, when I look at what a child actually does in the first few years, it's remarkable. A newborn can't even control its head. By about a year they're walking, by two they're manipulating objects, stacking blocks, pouring, and all of that is happening in a world that is not curated for them. The objects are novel, the lighting changes, the surfaces vary, they're growing so their own body is changing underneath them. And they do it with almost no explicit supervision. Nobody labels a million images for a baby. They learn from interaction, from trying things and seeing what happens, and a very small amount of social feedback.

So my way of understanding the difficulty is really to think about what's missing in our artificial systems. We've made a lot of progress in computer vision as a passive, pattern-recognition problem. But the child is not a passive observer. Vision is in service of action. The child moves its head to see better, reaches for something to find out what it is, and the perception and the control are co-developed. And I think that's the hard part, this closed loop between sensing and acting in a physical world that is high-dimensional, partially observable, and where the consequences of your actions are real. When a robot has to do that, you very quickly discover that the problem isn't solved just because you have a good object detector.

The other thing I'd emphasize is the developmental sequence itself. Children don't learn everything at once. There's a curriculum, partly from the maturation of the body and the nervous system, partly from the environment. Locomotion comes before fine manipulation, gross reaching before precision grasping. I think that staging is not an accident. It's probably a way of making an intractable learning problem tractable. And that's something I find very suggestive for robotics, this idea that you don't attack the full problem head-on, you build up competencies in some sensible order, and each one makes the next one learnable.

astra-6.text:
I think we tend to underestimate those skills because we acquire them before we can reflect on how difficult they are. A child learns to see, to move around, to reach for an object and grasp it. We take all of that for granted. Yet each of those activities requires an extraordinary amount of intelligence: you have to interpret sensory information, act on the world, and adjust as the world responds.

Then we regard things like algebra or chess as intellectually difficult because we learn them consciously, with effort. But that is not necessarily a good measure of computational difficulty. In robotics, picking up an unfamiliar object can be much harder than doing a long calculation. So the abilities children acquire in their early years are not merely preliminary to intelligence. They are a central part of what we need to understand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we tend to underestimate these skills because we acquire them so early and perform them without conscious effort. A child learns to recognize objects, reach for them, pick them up, walk across a room—all of which require a remarkable coordination of perception and action. And then we regard something like algebra as difficult because we have to work at it consciously.

For robotics, that intuition is almost reversed. We can make a computer do symbolic calculations very well, but getting a robot to pick up an unfamiliar object reliably is still challenging. It has to understand enough about the object, its own body, and the consequences of its actions to adapt as things change.

So I would regard those early childhood abilities as major achievements of intelligence. Their apparent effortlessness is a property of the solution that biology has developed, rather than evidence that the underlying problem is easy.
